name: Jomon Sugi
age_estimate: age fiercely disputed, at least 2,170 years

location.address: Ooboku Trail (大株歩道), off the Arakawa Trail, Mount Miyanoura area, Yakushima, Kagoshima Prefecture

access: Restricted to a viewing deck about 15m from the trunk (built 1996 to protect the roots from foot traffic); visitors cannot walk up to it. Reached only via the Arakawa Trailhead, which is closed to private cars March-November: a reserved shuttle bus (round trip roughly 2,000 yen) runs from the Yakusugi Museum before dawn, plus a conservation/trail fee of 1,000-2,000 yen.
transport: No public transport to the trailhead itself beyond the seasonal reserved shuttle bus from the Yakusugi Museum car park; from there it is an 8-11 hour round-trip hike (sources vary, roughly 22km total, ~11km one way), mostly along a disused logging railway then a steep mountain trail, departing before dawn to finish by dusk.
verify_notes: Japan's most famous ancient tree and the anchor of Yakushima's UNESCO listing (1993), discovered/named 1966-68. AGE IS OPEN AND CONTESTED, do not resolve it: (1) a 1976 Kyushu University estimate using ring measurements and girth put it over 7,000 years, which is where the 7,200 figure and the 'Jomon' name (implying it dates to the Jomon period) come from; (2) later investigation raised the possibility it is a 'gattai-boku', 2-3 younger trees fused around an older core, with the outer wood radiocarbon-dated to roughly 2,700 years (the core itself was left unsampled, to protect the tree); (3) Gakushuin University radiocarbon dating of core-area material gave 1,920+/-150 years, i.e. an upper bound of about 2,170 years; (4) a Kagoshima University isozyme analysis argued it is NOT a fused tree but a single individual; (5) the island's own pyroclastic-flow history (Kikai caldera eruption ~7,300 years ago wiped out large vegetation across southern Kyushu) is used to argue the tree cannot be much older than 4,000-5,000 years, since regrowth could not have started for roughly 1,000 years after that event. The town of Yakushima's own tourism page states the range as 2,170-7,200 years and calls the upper figure a theory ('...という説もあるが'), with 2,170 as the chemically measured figure. Report both ends, name the disagreement, do not average or pick a side. Physical size also varies by source and era (height 22.2m per the town, vs 25.3-30m in older/other sources, likely reflecting crown dieback over decades; girth 16.1m per the town's current page vs 16.4m widely cited elsewhere) - note as a range, do not silently pick one. ALIVE: yes, actively monitored, protection deck built 1996, suffered bark-stripping vandalism in 2005 but survived; well documented as living in recent tourism/park sources. ACCESS IS THE HARD PART: this is not a stroll. 8-11 hour round trip depending on source (town/japan-guide.com say roughly 10 hours; other operators quote 10-11), about 22km along a disused logging railway bed and then a steep mountain trail, shuttle-bus-only access road (private cars banned March-November), reservation needed a day ahead, departs before dawn. The page must state this in hours, not softened. Anecdote for the writer: the tree's gnarled, low, thick-crowned form is itself evidence of survival, it was left uncut through centuries of logging (including the Edo-period yakusugi harvest that took most of the island's other giants) precisely because its twisted wood was judged unusable as lumber.

name: Kigensugi

location.address: Roadside on the Anbo Forest Road (安房林道, also signed as the Yodogawa Line), about 6km / 15 minutes' drive past Yakusugi Land toward the Yodogawa Trailhead

access: Free, no entry fee or permit needed; a viewing platform circles the tree. Reachable by private car (the only yakusugi on the island you can drive to), or by one of two daily round-trip buses between the Yaku Sugi Museum and Yakusugi Land that continue on to Kigensugi.
transport: By car: on the forest road about 15 minutes past Yakusugi Land. By bus: only two round trips a day serve this stop; most visitors arrive by rental car or taxi.
verify_notes: The most accessible ancient yakusugi on the island, and arguably the better entry point for this page than Jomon Sugi given the site's promise of a good afternoon out: no hike required, just a short drive and a walk around a platform. Girth 8.1m and elevation ~1,230m independently corroborated across the town's own tourism page, the Kyushu Forest Office (rinya.maff.go.jp, a national government source) and Wikidata; height is given as 19.5m by the town/prefecture tourism pages but 16.5m on Wikidata, note as a range rather than picking one. Age given consistently as 'roughly 3,000 years' (an estimate, not a measured figure; no source states its basis, likely comparison with other dated yakusugi of similar girth) so treat age_min/max as a loose estimate band, not a precise range. Name means 'Origin/Era Cedar', a reference to the estimated age reaching back to the start of an era. Coordinates from Wikidata (Q106318003) land exactly on the Anbo forest road (安房林道) per OSM reverse geocoding, consistent with every description of the tree standing right beside this road. Vitality: recent visitor reviews (2025) and the tree's continued presence on all current tourism materials confirm it is standing and accessible now; it hosts over a dozen epiphytic plant species on its trunk and limbs (yamaguruma, Yakushima rhododendron, rowan and others), worth a line in the story. An old stump and another aged cedar stand nearby the platform, per one visitor account, not verified further and not itself a candidate.

name: Buddha Sugi

location.address: On the いにしえの森コース (Ancient Forest / 50-minute course) in Yakusugi Land, roughly midway around the ~1.0km loop, near Arakawa Bridge

access: Paid entry to Yakusugi Land (small conservation fee, payable at the entrance); reached on the 50-minute 'Ancient Forest Course', a maintained boardwalk/stone path loop needing no special gear, no reservation required.
transport: By car or the Yakusugi Land shuttle bus from Miyanoura/Anbo; the tree itself is roughly a 25-30 minute walk into the 50-minute loop from the Yakusugi Land entrance.
verify_notes: Named for the Buddha-like face suggested by one of its many burls; also called Shakasugi (Shaka = Buddha). Designated a National Special Natural Monument. Girth given consistently as 8.0m (Wikidata and a 2012 visitor account both agree), though one aggregated source quoted 12.6m; treat 8.0m as the better-supported figure but note the discrepancy. Height 21.5m from multiple sources. Age 'estimated 1,800 years' repeated across sources without a stated basis (no growth-rate working shown), so kept as a vague estimate rather than tightened. VITALITY FLAG: multiple sources spanning 1989 to 2012 describe the trunk as hollow and the main body as weakened/declining, with only upper branches (possibly a separate epiphytic individual rooted on top) still vigorous. This appears to be a long-standing structural condition of this specific tree rather than a recent event, since it is described the same way 23 years apart and the tree still appears as a named stop on the current (2026) official Ministry of Environment route page and current tourism guides, with no news of it falling. No dated 2024-2026 report was found specifically confirming it still stands after the August 2024 typhoon that felled Yayoi Sugi nearby (see blocked list); flagging this gap rather than asserting confidently. LOCATION: only approximate, the loop trail's midpoint rather than a mapped tree-level coordinate; pin is Yakusugi Land's general coordinate as an honest anchor, not the trunk itself.

name: Daio Sugi, the Great King Cedar
age_estimate: more than 3,000 years, per Japan's Ministry of the Environment

location.address: Yakushima, Kumage District, Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan
location.neighbourhood: on the Yakusugi trails inland; the exact trailhead needs settling before publication

story: Before 1966 this was the biggest cedar anyone on Yakushima knew about. Japan's Ministry of the Environment records Daio Sugi, the Great King Cedar, at more than 3,000 years old, 24.7 metres tall with a trunk 11.1 metres round, and notes it was believed to be the largest yakusugi in existence until Jomon Sugi was found and named in the 1960s. Losing a title is a rare career for a tree. Most of them keep whatever they are given, and this one had held the crown for as long as anyone on the island had been counting. It kept the name, which means great king, and it kept the measurements, which are not far behind the tree that took the record: Jomon Sugi's trunk is 16.1 metres round against this one's 11.1, and Jomon Sugi is the shorter of the two. Both grew up in the same forest under the same threat. The Edo-period yakusugi harvest took most of the island's giants for roof shingles and temple timber, felling cedars that had stood a thousand years and more, and Jomon Sugi came through it only because its twisted trunk was judged useless as lumber. Nobody has recorded why this one was spared.
